title: Why fast (Matthew 6:16–18)
hook: Jesus says when you fast, not if: quietly, without a gloomy face

segments.voice: Yesterday: be still, harpu, let go and drop your hands, said in the middle of an earthquake. Your line was be still, and know. When did you drop your hands? Day one hundred forty-six.

Skipping lunch is easy to announce. "Oh, I'm not eating today." A little sigh. A small pause, in case anyone wants to ask why. Everyone knows someone who does their diet or their detox out loud. Now picture Jesus on a hillside in Galilee, teaching a crowd, and he gets to fasting. He doesn't explain it. He doesn't argue for it. He assumes it. Not if you fast. When. And then, just like with giving a few days ago, he goes straight for the performance. He describes people who go around looking hungry on purpose, faces smudged and gloomy, so everyone can tell how holy they are. And he says: do the opposite. Today's word is the practice he's talking about.
screen: `I'M NOT EATING TODAY. SIGH.` → `NOT IF YOU FAST. WHEN.` → `THE GLOOMY FACE.`

segments.voice: Fasting. Going without food, or some food, for a time, for the sake of prayer. The old English word fast meant to hold firm, and fasting is holding firm against your own appetite. Here's what Jesus says in Matthew six, in the King James Bible: "Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast." Then: "But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret." Wash your face. Do your hair. Look normal. The same pattern as giving in secret: if you do it for an audience, the audience is all you get. Jesus himself fasted. Before his ministry began, the gospels say he spent forty days in the wilderness and was hungry afterward. Moses fasted on the mountain. Elijah on his long walk. Esther asked her people to fast before she risked her life. It's woven all through the Bible, and Jesus stands inside that tradition. So why would anyone choose to be hungry? Christians give a few reasons. Hunger clears the head; it reminds you that you're a body, dependent, not in control. Every pang becomes a small bell calling you back to prayer. That's today's line: hunger can pray. Fasting also makes room: the time and money you'd spend on food can go to someone else. And it's a way of saying, with your whole body, that you mean it. A caution many churches give: fasting is not a diet, and it's not for everyone. People who are pregnant, ill or recovering from an eating disorder are usually told not to fast from food at all. Many choose to fast from something else instead.
screen: `FAST: TO HOLD FIRM.` · `WASH THY FACE. LOOK NORMAL.` · `MOSES, ELIJAH, ESTHER, JESUS.` · `EVERY PANG A SMALL BELL.` · then, large: `WHEN YE FAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Not a fast today, just a small taste of the idea. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small comfort you reach for without thinking: the second coffee, the snack at three, the scroll before bed, the sugar in your tea. Pick one. Just one, for today. Now imagine the moment tomorrow afternoon when you'll want it and won't have it. Instead of the thing, you'll have a small ache. If you pray, you can let that ache become a short prayer. If you don't, let it be a moment of noticing. The bell holds the time.
Fasting. Going without for a while, for the sake of prayer. Jesus says when, not if, and quietly, with a washed face.
Your line: hunger can pray. Today, skip one small comfort, tell nobody, and let the little ache point somewhere. Day one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Many Christians fast by skipping meals or certain foods on set days or seasons, spending the time in prayer, and many give up a comfort instead when fasting from food isn't safe for them.

trapdoor: what you thought: fasting is a diet with a halo.
what it means: going without for the sake of prayer, quietly, with a washed face, so hunger becomes a bell.
what a scholar hears: Jesus's hearers already fasted; his teaching is about how. the Greek nēsteia, and Old English fæstan, to hold firm.

notes: Etymology: English 'fast' (abstain) from Old English fæstan, related to fæst, firm; 'to hold firm' is a common gloss. Confirm.
Elijah's 40 days (1 Kings 19:8) is on the strength of one meal rather than a stated fast; script says 'Elijah on his long walk'. Confirm.
Health caution: reflects common pastoral guidance; confirm wording is appropriate and not medical advice.
Matthew 6:17–18 quotation ends mid-verse ('which is in secret'); confirm.
